# Language & Communication

_Applies when: always — choosing the language for prose vs. code._

Derived from the user's own rule and board files (consistently German prose).

## Default to German for humans

- Chat replies, explanations, plans, commit bodies, scrum stories, and ADR narrative default to
  **German**; switch to English only when the user writes in English or explicitly asks. UI copy is German.
- **A German commit subject begins lowercase** — deliberately **stricter than the gate**: `subject-case`
  rejects only a capital first letter (`sentence-case` is `upperFirst(input)`, no `toLowerCase`), so
  acronyms mid-subject pass and a subject not starting with a cased letter is never checked at all.
- German display text uses real umlauts (ä ö ü Ä Ö Ü ß), never the ASCII stand-ins ue/ae/oe/ss —
  everywhere a human reads (JSX text, aria/title/alt/placeholder, error/toast, PWA manifest, `<title>`,
  native window/tray titles). Files are UTF-8, so the stand-ins are a habit, not a constraint — enforce real umlauts with a gate or the habit creeps back.

## Keep code in English

- Identifiers, code comments, file/branch names, and Conventional-Commit subject prefixes (`feat:`,
  `fix:`, …) stay **English**, as do technical terms with no clean German equivalent — don't invent
  awkward translations.
- Code stays ASCII even when its display text carries umlauts (identifiers, variables, route paths, CSS
  classes, file names, test IDs, JSON keys): a variable `raeumeLabel` holding the display text 'Räume' is
  correct — renaming the identifier too is the mistake. Never blind-replace `ue→ü` (it destroys `value`, `queue`, `true`, `unique`); substitute only from a vetted whole-word list.
